title: What the Return of Measles Means for the U.S.
author: Alice Park
body:
On Nov. 17, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) declared that measles is no longer considered "eliminated" in the U.S. In the past year, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recorded more than 5,800 cases of measles—the highest caseload since 1991.

Vaccination programs and increased monitoring of incoming measles cases helped the U.S. to eliminate measles in 2000, meaning there was no consistent spread of the virus within the country for more than a year. Since then, sporadic cases of the virus have been reported—but from people who had traveled to other parts of the world where the disease is endemic.

No longer. So far, the CDC reports that 47 states have reported at least one case of measles, and wastewater reports of cases of the virus have increased in recent months. “What makes this different from pop-up cases that we expect year to year is that we failed to interrupt the chain of transmission of the virus,” says Steph Batalis, research fellow at Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology. “That’s a big deal. We have tools to do that, yet we failed to do so. That should raise serious questions about the conditions that allowed that to happen.”

Days after the announcement, Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) Robert F. Kennedy Jr. posted on X that HHS will "work to regain U.S. measles elimination status. I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles.”

While Kennedy went on to blame COVID for interrupting childhood vaccinations, public-health officials point to several other more recent actions that Kennedy, a long-time skeptic of vaccines, has taken that may have also contributed to the rise of measles cases in the U.S. In 2025, Kennedy dismissed the CDC’s Advisory Committee for Immunization Practices, an independent group of experts that sets vaccine recommendations for the U.S. that state health departments and professional organizations generally follow, and replaced the committee with members who shared his vaccine skepticism. HHS also attempted to revise the childhood immunization schedule, removing recommendations for most children to receive annual flu and COVID shots, and emphasizing shared-decision making about vaccines between families and physicians. Professional health organizations—including the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American College of Physicians, and the Infectious Diseases Society of America—sued HHS over these changes. A court suspended the new ACIP from continuing to meet and reverted the childhood immunization schedule back to its original recommendations.

Such confusion around vaccines has likely played a significant role in the U.S. measles outbreaks of the past year, says Dr. Jon Andrus, professor of global health at the Milken Institute School of Public Health at George Washington University. “Any successful public-health program requires excellence in scientific and operational strategies about how you are vaccinating, when you vaccinate them, and what vaccines you use, all based on evidence,” he says. “And none of that works without political commitment. If that is undermined, and if the messages coming from the highest level sows seeds of doubt, then you have people doubting the strategies and not vaccinating their child.”

He and other public-health experts say that the loss of the measles elimination status isn’t merely a symbolic change. It’s a warning sign of a weakened public-health system fueled by deteriorating trust in scientific experts and mixed messages from health leaders who the public normally turn to for advice. And the change in the U.S.’s status may have deeper consequences for public health, beyond just more cases of measles.

Here's what's worrying experts.

There are long-term consequences of getting measles

Some of the public’s attitudes about vaccines—including the one for measles, which is part of the MMR series—center around unsubstantiated claims that the vaccines contain toxic chemicals that do more harm than good, and that the measles shot in particular is linked to a higher risk of autism, a claim that has for years been scientifically debunked. Because measles has not been common in the U.S. for decades, a generation of parents and doctors have not seen how devastating the disease can be.

“Measles in Latin means ‘miserable,’” says Andrus. Having measles can cause pneumonia, ear infections, and encephalitis, or brain swelling. But even if a child recovers from a measles infection, the disease may affect his or her health for years to come. “Measles infections can contribute to deafness, blindness, and, depending on the neurological insult, intellectual and physical disability as well,” says Dr. Micah Niermann, an internal medicine and pediatric physician at Gillette Children’s in St. Paul, Minn. “Some may need lifelong care, and their lives and the lives of their families are altered permanently.”

More recently, scientists have also uncovered another way the virus can impact a person’s health, even if they recover from the infection. “The measles virus can attack immune cells and make them less effective for some prolonged period of time,” says Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics. “We don’t know how long, but for that period after measles, the child is more susceptible to other kinds of infections that they are ordinarily immune to.” The measles virus has the ability to wipe out whatever memory the immune cells have accumulated to recognize other pathogens—including those introduced by vaccines. “A child who has had measles is at risk of suffering from or dying from other vaccine-preventable diseases, and that risk goes out three years or longer,” says Andrus.

There is also a rare but still meaningful risk of longer term consequences of measles known as subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a condition caused by the measles virus destroying brain cells. SSPE’s symptoms can start years after a measles infection but cannot be triggered by the measles vaccine. Children may start to show changes in personality and experience seizures or involuntary movements of their arms and legs, which then leads to dementia and problems eating, swallowing, and breathing. The condition is almost always fatal. Children under two who get measles are at higher risk of developing SPPE later in life, and the best way to prevent the condition is to protect those children from getting measles in the first place with the vaccine, or for those too young to be vaccinated, to ensure those around them are vaccinated so they are less likely to get exposed to measles.

Some people may need a booster shot

Most adults who have received two doses of the MMR vaccine do not need to get a booster; the two doses provide 97% protection against infection for a lifetime, according to the CDC. Most people who were born before 1957 also don’t need an additional shot since they were likely exposed to measles because there was no vaccine yet available.

The only groups that may need to consider a booster are people who might not know if they received two doses of the vaccine or people who are immunocompromised, such as those undergoing chemotherapy. They might benefit from the booster after, but not while, they are undergoing chemotherapy, to give their immune systems additional support. “Say you are undergoing a bone marrow transplant or chemotherapy: this adds another element of risk assessment for patients,” says Niermann. “There are people at risk who could get ill from measles.”

Another group of people who should consider a booster are those born from 1963 to 1967. In that time, an old version of the vaccine was used that might not be as effective as the current version, which relies on a weakened, live version of the measles virus. People who are currently 59-63 should discuss with their health care provider whether they need a booster.

Outbreaks won't stop at measles

“Measles is the canary in the coal mine,” says Racine. “This is not just about measles. The reason we’re seeing measles first is that it’s more contagious than any other infectious disease." If one person is infected, for instance, 90% of people in close contact with that person can get infected as well. And the virus can stay airborne from an infected person’s cough or sneeze for up to two hours.

"It’s as if measles is knocking on the door of every household in the country saying, ‘Guess what, I’m here. I’m back,'" Racine says. "'You may have thought I got lost and went someplace else. I’m here to tell you that you forgot to lock the door, and I’m coming in. And not only that, but I’m not by myself. Take a look behind me, I’ve brought a bunch of friends: influenza, hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae, pertussis, whooping cough. Look down the list, and you see polio back there too. They’re coming—we’re all coming.’”

Measles is so contagious that it’s often the first outbreak public-health experts see as childhood vaccination rates decline. “We often say that measles outbreaks are a signal of a weaker immunization system,” says Dr. William Moss, professor at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. “This is a red flag and tells us we’re not doing what we need to be doing to control measles.” As vaccination rates fall in general, other vaccine-preventable diseases will start to spike. “I will be surprised if we don’t start to see more cases of congenital rubella and mumps,” says Dr. Wendy Armstrong, president of the Infectious Diseases Society of America and head of the division of infectious diseases at the University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine.

Measles outbreaks could threaten U.S. biosecurity

The measles outbreak may also affect the U.S.’s ability to protect itself from infectious threats.

The health care costs associated with measles—in terms of immediate care and the potential longer terms consequences if they develop SPPE—are already burdening overstretched local and state health resources. Doctors and public-health experts who could be dedicated to focusing on other threats are now required to manage preventable illnesses. “Public-health departments are on the front lines, and if they are addressing measles outbreaks, which is something that is avoidable, then there are opportunity costs for how they are able to address other issues,” says Niermann.

Even more concerning, says Batalis, are the mixed messages coming from federal health authorities. “If people are looking to get [health] information for themselves, the question becomes: Who is filling that vacuum of information?” she says. “If it’s not filled by trustworthy sources and if the government is discrediting trustworthy sources, then who fills the gap? Now we’re seeing reports that a lot of vaccine disinformation is coming from bots, which raises a lot of questions about how that makes us more vulnerable, and how could adversaries exploit that. There is a security consideration in addition to public health.”

How can the U.S. regain its status as having eliminated measles?

“The very first thing that needs to happen is a recognition that an error has been made,” says Racine. “And unfortunately, in the condition that we’re currently in, the folks who are in charge of this have not been willing or able to recognize that a mistake has been made here. Until that happens, we are not able to have the full force of all the government authorities—from local, state, and national levels—working in conjunction with pediatricians and the community and public-health officials to seriously address what is going on.”

While CDC director Erica Schwartz has said that the CDC is deploying resources to areas experiencing measles outbreaks, Racine says those cases will continue to spread if there isn’t a stronger and more unified message about the best way to control measles: by supporting vaccination and reiterating that it is safe. While both Kennedy and Schwartz have said they support measles vaccines, Kennedy has also stated that protection from the vaccine “waned quickly” and that the shot has not been “safely tested”—positions not supported by scientific evidence.

“There are going to be long-term consequence of what is happening today,” says Racine.
